laws.rule: Required: respect sacred places and ceremonies, dress modestly at temples and public places, use licensed guides, licensed money changers, pay in rupiah (QRIS), and use legal transport and accommodation. laws.rule: Governor's Circular 7/2025 (March 2025) updates Circular 4/2023. It adds that foreign tourists must follow Indonesian traffic rules, carry a valid international or national driving licence, wear a helmet on a motorbike, not overload vehicles, use officially registered four-wheel transport and not drive under the influence of alcohol or drugs. It also asks tourists to pay the levy and to be accompanied by a licensed guide at attractions. Residents can report tourists' breaches to a provincial hotline.
laws.penalty_signal: Sanctions or legal process under Indonesian law

laws.rule: Under Governor's Circular 7/2025: dress modestly at temples and ceremonies, use licensed money changers and follow traffic rules. Prohibited: working or doing business without permits, illegal drugs, littering, stepping on or damaging offerings, inappropriate photos or disrespectful behaviour in sacred areas, and excessive, aggressive or impolite bargaining. Foreign tourists must pay the IDR 150,000 levy (about A$11.74, RBA rate of 30 October 2026) via the Love Bali website.

laws.rule: Under Bali Provincial Regulation 6 of 2023, every foreign tourist entering Bali, whether directly from abroad or through another part of Indonesia, must pay an electronic levy of IDR 150,000 (about A$11.74 at the RBA rate of 30 October 2026). The payment is made once, before or on arrival at a Bali entry point, and remains valid until the visitor leaves Indonesia. Visitors who cannot show proof of payment must pay then; those who still do not pay are forbidden from touring Bali. The regulation took effect on 14 February 2024. The official Love Bali FAQ, which cites the 2025 amendment (Provincial Regulation 2 of 2025) and Governor Regulation 25 of 2025, confirms the amount is still IDR 150,000 and lists exemptions for holders of diplomatic and official visas, transport crew, KITAS or KITAP holders, family-unification and student visas, and (on application through the Love Bali system) golden visas and other visas. Cruise passengers also pay, individually or through a registered agent.

layers.process: Every foreign tourist (anyone from outside Indonesia who isn't an Indonesian citizen and is touring in Bali) pays a levy of IDR 150,000 per person, about A$11.74 at the RBA rate of 30 October 2026 (A$1 = IDR 12,780). The money funds protection of Bali's culture and natural environment, and it's separate from the visa or e-VOA. Payment is cashless: online through Love Bali before arrival, or at the counters on arrival at the airport or seaport, during the stay, or on departure; counter staff use your passport to fill in the details. The voucher is emailed, and the system checks for duplicate payments. The Love Bali site also takes exemption applications. The official Love Bali FAQ lists exemptions for holders of diplomatic and official visas, transport crew, KITAS or KITAP holders, family-unification and student visas, and (on application through Love Bali) golden visas and other visas. Visitors who cannot show proof of payment must pay; those who still do not pay are forbidden from touring Bali under Provincial Regulation 6 of 2023 (official PDF on the Love Bali site).

culture-and-protocol.dress_and_conduct: Under Governor's Circular 4 of 2023, foreign tourists must respect the sanctity of temples, pratima and religious symbols; respect customs and ceremonies in progress; wear polite, appropriate clothing at sacred places, attractions and in public; behave politely; use a licensed guide at attractions; pay in rupiah (QRIS for QR payments) and change money only at licensed changers; ride with a valid licence, a helmet and modest clothing; and stay in licensed accommodation.
culture-and-protocol.sacred_or_restricted_places: Tourists must not enter the main (utama) or middle (madya) mandala of temples except to pray in Balinese dress, and not while menstruating; must not climb sacred trees or sacred buildings, or pose for photos in improper dress or naked at sacred places; must not litter or use single-use plastic; and must not be rude or aggressive, work without permits or deal in illegal goods including drugs. Breaches can bring sanctions or prosecution under Indonesian law.
